intro: People often sort political ideas along a line from left to right. That line is a helpful start, but it hides a lot. Two people who use the same label may want very different things. Two people with different labels may agree on more than they expect. In this unit you will look closely at the main ideas that shape politics in Europe, the Americas and beyond.

You will meet the thinkers behind these ideas, such as John Locke, Adam Smith, John Stuart Mill, Edmund Burke and Karl Marx. You will see how liberalism, conservatism, socialism, social democracy, libertarianism and nationalism grew from real problems in real places. For each one, you will hear what supporters say and what critics say.

By the end, you will be able to explain what each idea stands for, compare two ideas fairly, and notice when a word means different things in different countries. You will also be able to use evidence to build and defend your own argument while treating other views with respect.
bigQuestion: How do different political ideas answer the question of how people should live together, and what do their supporters and critics say?

timeline.t: John Locke publishes the Second Treatise of Government on natural rights.
Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations, arguing for free markets.
Edmund Burke publishes Reflections on the Revolution in France.
Marx and Engels publish The Communist Manifesto.
John Stuart Mill publishes On Liberty and the harm principle.
Italy is unified as a kingdom; Germany follows in 1871.
The Bolsheviks seize power in Russia, leading to the Soviet Union.
The U.S. creates Social Security as part of the New Deal.
India wins independence from Britain after a long nonviolent movement.
Konrad Adenauer becomes West Germany's first chancellor.
Ghana becomes independent, inspiring movements across Africa.

words.d: rights people have simply because they are human, not because a ruler grants them
a set of ideas that stresses individual rights, free markets and limited government
Mill's rule that society may limit a person's freedom only to prevent harm to others
a government that provides programs like pensions, health care and unemployment help
a political view that values tradition, gradual change and long-standing institutions
the idea that problems should be handled by the smallest group able to handle them well
a person who wants government kept very small to protect the widest individual freedom
the idea that major resources should be owned or controlled by the public or the community
Marx's idea that history is driven by conflict between owners and workers

test.q: Which thinker wrote that government exists to protect life, liberty and property?
test.why: Locke's Second Treatise of Government (1690) named these natural rights.

test.q: What did Adam Smith mean by the invisible hand?
choices: Self-interest in a free market can end up helping society
test.why: Smith used the image to describe how markets turn private effort into public benefit.

test.q: Which situation would Mill's harm principle allow the government to stop?
choices: A person eating unhealthy food at home
A speaker sharing an unpopular opinion
A person choosing an unusual hobby
A person damaging a neighbor's property
test.why: The harm principle permits limits on freedom only to prevent harm to others.

test.q: Which statement best describes Burke's conservatism?
choices: Change should be sudden and total
Change should be gradual and respect tradition
test.why: Burke favored careful, step-by-step reform that keeps the wisdom of institutions.

test.q: Which program is an example of the welfare state?
test.why: The NHS, founded in 1948, provides public health care, a core welfare state program.

test.q: How does a U.S. liberal usually differ from a European liberal?
choices: The U.S. liberal wants a king
The U.S. liberal usually favors more government programs
test.why: Since the New Deal, American liberals usually favor more government action, while many European liberals favor markets.

test.q: Which idea comes from Christian democracy?
test.why: Postwar West German Christian democrats called their mix of markets and social programs a social market economy.

test.q: What do libertarians and classical liberals share?
choices: A strong focus on individual liberty and limited government
Belief that traditions must never change
test.why: Libertarianism takes classical liberal ideas of limited government to their fullest form.

test.q: In Marx's terms, who owns the factories and capital?
test.why: Marx called the owning class the bourgeoisie and the working class the proletariat.

test.q: Which is part of the real record of twentieth-century communist states?
choices: Famine during China's Great Leap Forward
test.why: Most historians estimate tens of millions died in the famine of 1958 to 1962.

test.q: Which country is an example of the Nordic model?
test.why: Denmark, Sweden and Norway combine market economies with high taxes and large welfare states.

test.q: What is the key difference between social democracy and democratic socialism?
choices: How much of the economy should be publicly owned
test.why: Social democrats keep most business private; democratic socialists want much more public ownership.

test.q: Which leader used nonviolent resistance to seek independence?
test.why: Gandhi led marches and boycotts, such as the 1930 Salt March, against British rule.

test.q: What turned nationalism dangerous in Nazi Germany?
choices: Racism, hatred of outsiders and conquest
test.why: Nazi extreme nationalism rested on racism and led to the Holocaust and World War II.

test.q: Which statement fits the scholarly definition of populism?
choices: It exists only on the left
It is the same as conservatism
It sets a pure people against a corrupt elite
test.why: Cas Mudde defines populism as a thin set of ideas that pits the people against the elite.

write.prompt: Should a government do more to share wealth, or should it leave more to individuals and markets? Take a position. Use two or three facts, thinkers or sources from this unit, and explain the strongest point on the other side.
tips: Name your sources, such as Locke, Smith, Mill, Burke, Marx or the OECD figures.
Give the other side fairly, in words its supporters would accept.
Use the unit's terms, like welfare state, social democracy or minimal state.
Explain why your evidence supports your claim, not just what it says.
